newsitem.title: INDIA: India faulted for focusing on belt-tightening.
newsitem.headline: India faulted for focusing on belt-tightening.

text.p: A new U.N. report released on Thursday faults India's commitment to reducing red ink and says the policy has led to the "abdication of state responsibilities in key areas".
The 1997 Human Development Report commissioned annually by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) gives India mixed grades for reducing poverty during its nearly 50 years of independence.
The report commends India for progress in agriculture, industry and, more recently, poverty reduction.
"But the record is mixed -- and India remains a country of stark contrasts and disparities," it said.
Between 1951 and 1995, food grain production increased four-fold and famines were virtually eliminated, it said. But 53 percent of children under four -- some 60 million -- remain undernourished.
In 1961-91, literacy more than doubled, but half the population is still illiterate.
During three decades until 1992, life expectancy almost doubled to 61 years, and by 1995 infant mortality had more than halved to 74 per 1,000 live births.
"Even so, each year there are 2.2 million infant deaths, most of them avoidable," the 245-page report said.
The UNDP report, released worldwide on Thursday, said national statistics masked wide variation among regions and states.

Four states have managed to reduce income poverty by more than 50 percent since 1951 -- Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Kerala and Punjab. But 50 percent of India's rural poor live in three states -- Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
The report, citing the government's plan to eradicate poverty by 2005, says there are reasons for optimism.
The policies for wiping out poverty focus on human development priorities -- basic health, education, safe drinking water and special attention to socially disadvantaged groups, it said.
Since free-market reforms were introduced, economic conditions have been more favourable, it said.
But the report said there was also cause for concern.

"The focus on reducing fiscal deficits is forcing major cuts in public spending, and the emphasis on state minimalism is leading to abdication of state responsibilities in key areas affecting the lives of poor people," it said.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's centre-left government has vowed to cut the fiscal deficit as a share of gross domestic product, which stood at 5.0 percent at the end of 1996/97 (April-March), to 4.5 percent in 1997/98.
The government argues that a lower fiscal deficit will spur investment and economic growth, and bring down interest rates.

The U.N.-commissioned report said the government was failing to provide free and compulsory elementary education, abolish child labour, provide adequately for the security of marginalised communities and improve living conditions in slums.
